div.head: Introduction:
div.p: We present the case of a 58-year-old female with Branchiootorenal (BOR) syndrome who was diagnosed with glioblastoma (GBM). A relationship between BOR syndrome and GBM has not previously been reported, prompting a literature review into the underlying genomics of BOR syndrome and CNS glioma. Case Presentation: The patient underwent craniotomy for resection with pathology demonstrating IDH-wildtype (WHO grade 4), MGMT-unmethylated glioblastoma. After outpatient discussion with oncology, the patient and her family elected not to pursue chemotherapy or radiation. Conclusion: Literature review revealed common mutations to EYA and SIX genes, suggesting a possible unestablished relationship and future pathway for targeted treatments. Future studies should investigate the incidence of glioma in BOR patients with emphasis on genetic testing.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: We present the case of a 58-year-old female with Branchiootorenal (BOR) syndrome who was diagnosed with glioblastoma (GBM) after craniotomy for resection of right temporal and thalamic to midbrain mass. A relationship between BOR syndrome and GBM has not previously been reported. Literature review revealed common mutations to EYA and SIX genes in the development of BOR syndrome and primary CNS glioma, suggesting a possible association.

div.head: Case Presentation
div.p: The patient was admitted for alcohol intoxication with concern for seizure-like activity secondary to malnutrition. She developed rapidly progressive left hemiparesis and hypoesthesia, recurrent falls, and headache, prompting admission and further evaluation over several weeks. Prior to her presentation, the patient's only known medical history was a diagnosis of BOR syndrome, alcohol abuse, and anxiety. No additional significant family history was reported prior to the patient's death.

She was transferred to our facility after imaging demonstrated an intracranial mass with 2 components: a right temporal with peripheral enhancement and central T2 hyperintensity (3 × 4.7 × 3.2 cm) and a thalamic/midbrain component with irregular enhancement (6.0 × 4.4 × 3.5 cm) (Fig. 1). Subsequent metastatic work-up was negative. She underwent craniotomy for subtotal resection due to the proximity to corticospinal tracts of the thalamic mass on subcortical stimulation. Pathology demonstrated IDH-wildtype (WHO grade 4), MGMT-unmethylated glioblastoma. Histology noted high mitotic activity, extensive necrosis, and vascular proliferation and luminal thrombosis (Fig. 2). Postoperatively, she developed hydrocephalus, necessitating ventriculoperitoneal shunt prior to discharge to inpatient rehabilitation. After outpatient discussion with oncology, the patient and her family elected not to pursue chemotherapy or radiation. She entered hospice care and died 2 months postoperatively.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: BOR is an autosomal dominant disorder with variable expression among family members characterized by hearing loss, structural defects of the ear, brachial fistulas or cysts, and renal abnormalities [1]. In 2004, Chang et al. [2] presented clinical diagnostic criteria based on patients with EYA1 mutation. Patients must have 3 major criteria, 2 major criteria and 2 minor criteria, or 1 major criterion and a first-degree relative meeting criterion. Major criteria include branchial anomalies, deafness, preauricular pits, and renal anomalies. There are no significant clinical differences between BOR syndrome patients with EYA1 mutations and those with less common mutations, such as SIX1 and SIX 5 [3]. The prevalence of BOR syndrome is not well characterized with one study estimating a 2% prevalence in profoundly deaf children [1].

BOR syndrome is attributed to 3 known gene mutations: EYA1 in 40%, SIX5 in 2.5%, and SIX1 in 2%. Mutations of the EYA1 gene are diverse and genetically heterogenous in BOR syndrome, ranging from large deletions to more complex rearrangements [2,4,5]. The four EYA proteins (EYA1-4) are mammalian homologous of the Drosophila eyes absent (eya) gene, which interact with a Drosophila homolog of SIX, So, as part of a critical network for eye development in Drosophila [6]. Given their intrinsic phosphatase activity, EYA serves as a promotor-specific transcription coactivator within the SIX-EYA-DACH network. This network is essential in development and organogenesis. SIX is a transcription factor that requires EYA family cofactor for activation. It may act as a transcriptional activator or repressor depending on the cofactors involved. SIX binds with EYA proteins to induce nuclear translocation of the protein complex and recruitment of other coactivators. Yet, EYA1 has intrinsic phosphatase activity and, therefore, the capacity to act independently [7]. After completion of organ development, SIX1 is downregulated, and its expression is low or non-detectable in adults [8].

The EYA, SIX, and its associated complex have been implicated in a variety of cancers. Reor overexpression of Eya proteins has been implicated in the oncogenesis of numerous cancers including breast, ovarian, lung, medulloblastoma, GBM, leukemia, and Wilm's tumor [9]. The importance of EYA and SIX protein cooperativity has been demonstrated in breast cancer. High expression of both SIX1 and EYA2 correlated with increased relapse and metastasis rates, yet tumors with high SIX1 but low EYA2 did not show this relationship [10].

There has been increased interest in understanding the role of EYA1 and SIX1 in glial tumors. Analysis of chromatin regulation genes in 194 astrocytoma patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas database demonstrated that EYA1 was significantly higher in IDH mutant gliomas [11]. Auvergne et al. [12] utilized mRNA profiling to identify and compare genes between glial progenitor cells (GPCs) from normal brain tissue and tumor-initiating progenitor cells (TPCs) isolated from human gliomas (WHO grade II-IV). They noted dysregulation of transcription factor SIX1 and its cofactors, EYA1 and DACH2. SIX1 and EYA1 were overexpressed ≥10-fold in cells from both low-and high-grade glioma compared to their non-tumor GPCs. shRNA silencing of SIX1 inhibited TPCs in vitro and in vivo. Kim et al. [13] also found that EYA1 was preferentially expressed in GBM stem cells compared to differentiated tumor progeny. Reducing EYA1 expression via lentiviral transduction hindered sphere formation in vitro, and EYA1 knockdown increased tumor latency with prolonged survival in tumor-bearing mice. These studies suggest that EYA1 and SIX1 may be a therapeutic target in glial oncogenesis and progression.

Additionally, EYA1 has been identified as a positive regulator of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling via coupling with SIX1 to promote gene induction in response to SHH. An estimated 30% of all medulloblastomas, one of the most common primary pediatric brain tumors, are driven by gain-of-function mutations in the SHH signaling pathway with EYA1 demonstrating high expression in this subtype [14]. Hwang et al. [15] recently developed an allosteric

div.head: Case Reports in Oncology
div.p: inhibitor of EYA proteins, which successfully functioned as an EYA antagonist in medulloblastoma cell lines via opposing SHH signaling and inhibited cell growth in vitro and in vivo. Excellent brain penetration allowed for increased lifespan in mice predisposed to SHH medulloblastoma, demonstrating significant promise for future therapy targeting EYA1.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: BOR syndrome is closely related to loss of function mutations of the SIX-EYA complex, while overexpression has been shown in multiple cancer types, including GBM, to promote tumorigenesis. Our case of GBM in a patient with BOR may represent a coincidence or an unestablished relationship pertaining to EYA/SIX genes. Unfortunately, genetic testing for EYA/SIX mutations was not performed for our patient prior to her death. A causal relationship, such as loss of function mutation leading to upregulation/dysregulation of related pathways, is possible, albeit hypothetical. Future studies should investigate the incidence of glioma in BOR patients with emphasis on genetic testing, although would be challenging given the low prevalence of BOR syndrome. Further understanding of the SIX-EYA pathways may provide important targets for the treatment of gliomas.

div.head: Statement of Ethics
div.p: This retrospective review of patient data did not require ethical approval in accordance with local guidelines. No ethics approval was required from our Institutional Review Board and OSF Research Committee. Given the patient is deceased, her next of kin/power of attorney was contacted and written informed consent was obtained for publication of the details of the medical case and any accompanying images. The CARE Checklist has been completed by the authors for this case report and attached as online supplementary material (for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/006541677).
